title: TA9-10599
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXXXXXX, the claimant, alleges he is a citizen of the People's Republic of China (PRC). He claims refugee protection pursuant to section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (IRPA).

The claimant alleges that he began practicing Falun Gong with his parents in 1994. He alleges that when the Chinese government banned the practice of Falun Gong in 1999 he was ordered to stop practicing Falun Gong by security and government officials. When he initially refused to give up his practice he alleges that he was detained in a room for the day until he finally agreed. The claimant, however, did not stop practicing Falun Gong but began to practice in secret. In XXXXX 2009, the claimant alleges that he received a telephone call advising him that a member of his Falun Gong group had been arrested by members of the Public Security Bureau (PSB) and that he should go into hiding. Fearing that he would be arrested, the claimant used the services of a smuggler to leave China for Canada where he filed for refugee protection.

The issue of late submission of documents to the Board was raised by the Panel at the start of the hearing. It was noted by the panel that the claimant filed his Personal Information Form (PIF) in June 2009. However, the claimant did not provide any other corroborating documents to the Board until October 5, 2011, six days prior to the hearing. It was pointed out to counsel that the late submission of the documents was not in compliance with Refugee Protection Division Rules. Counsel for the claimant advised the panel that she provided the documents shortly after receiving them. The claimant's explanation for filing late documents was that the first letter he received from the Board concerning the submission of documents was "expired" and that he was waiting for a second letter before he submitted the documents. While the panel was not persuaded by the claimant's explanation, the documents submitted are central to his claim. As such, the panel accepted the late submission of documents as evidence in the hearing.
The panel finds that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The reasons are as follows.
The claimant's identity as a national of the People's Republic of China is established by his Resident Identity Card2 which was tendered into evidence.

The determinative issue in this claim is the claimant's identity as a genuine practitioner of Falun Gong. The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant's testimony in this regard is not credible. The reasons for this finding are noted below.

In assessing credibility, the panel was mindful of the claimant's age, education and background. The claimant alleges he has 11 years of formal education in China. In addition, the panel is cognizant of the many difficulties faced by a claimant in establishing a claim, including cultural factors, the milieu of the hearing room, and the stress inherent in responding to oral questions through an interpreter and nervousness.

Credibility is an issue in all claims before the Immigration and Refugee Board. In order to determine whether the claim is well founded, the panel must find, on a balance of probabilities, that the evidence is credible and trustworthy. A claimant's testimony is presumed to be true unless there are valid reasons to doubt its truthfulness.3 The existence of contradictions, discrepancies and implausibilities in the evidence of a claimant is a well-accepted basis for a finding of a lack of credibility. This also applies to omissions in the claimant's previous statements, whether made to Canadian immigration officials at the time of arrival in Canada, in previous examinations under oath or at the hearing of the claim, or in the claimant's Personal Information Form (PIF). The panel finds that there were numerous instances of contradictions, omissions and discrepancies with the claimant's testimony and PIF. In the context of the numerous contradictions, omissions and discrepancies, the panel can give little weight to the claimant's testimony and finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the overall credibility of the claimant is undermined.

The claimant testified that he went into hiding after learning that his fellow Falun Gong group member had been arrested while distributing flyers. The claimant testified that he feared he would be arrested because he also distributed Falun Gong flyers. The claimant was asked why he failed to mention is his PIF that the arrest was related to the distribution of flyers. The claimant responded that he "didn't dare mention" the distribution of flyers because he was uncertain of the situation in Canada. He further alleged that when he lived in China he was aware that there were Chinese government spies in Canada and he was concerned what would happen if he spoke about the distribution of flyers. The panel rejects that claimant's explanation. The claimant made his refugee claim on XXXXX, 2009, and filed his PIF on June 16, 2009. However, the claimant testified that on XXXXX, 2009, five days prior to making a refugee protection claim, he attended a Falun Gong protest in front of the Chinese consulate in Toronto. The claimant's testimony is inconsistent with his alleged actions. The panel finds it neither plausible nor credible that claimant would consider the mentioning of the distribution of flyers in his PIF too risky given his alleged participation in the demonstration almost six weeks previous.

In addition, the basis for the claimant's alleged fear of the PSB is founded in his allegation that he distributed flyers. As such, the panel finds it unreasonable that he would have failed to include in his PIF the very reason he feared the PSB. In this regard, the panel draws a negative inference.

The claimant alleged that he came to Canada to flee persecution of Chinese authorities. The panel asked the claimant why he would come to Canada if he was uncertain of "the situation" in Canada for practitioners of Falun Gong. The claimant responded that he "did not feel at ease" when he first came to Canada but later learned that the Canadian government could protect him. The panel rejects that claimant's testimony in this regard. The panel also finds neither plausible nor credible that the claimant would participate in a public Falun Gong demonstration in front of the Chinese consulate if he was uncertain of "the situation" of Falun Gong practitioners in Canada.

The panel pointed out to the claimant that his testimony was inconsistent in this regard. The claimant responded that he was not afraid to demonstrate. He alleged that he only found out later that the Chinese consulate would have cameras. The panel notes that no evidence was adduced to support his claim that Falun Gong practitioners were under surveillance by Chinese authorities in Canada in 2010. Additionally, the claimant contradicted himself when he later testified that he was aware that there was likelihood that he would be identified if he demonstrated in front of the Chinese consulate. In addition, the claimant's testimony is inconsistent with his testimony that he was aware prior to demonstrating that Chinese government had spies operating in Canada. In this regard, the panel draws a negative inference.

The claimant was questioned later in the hearing by his counsel and asked about his attendance at demonstrations outside the Chinese consulate. In answering counsel, the claimant testified that he was initially frightened to demonstrate but later became less concerned about demonstrating. The claimant's testimony in this regard is inconsistent with his earlier testimony in which he stated that he was not afraid to demonstrate. The panel draws a negative inference from the claimant's inconsistent testimony.

The claimant was asked to explain why he felt that mentioning the distribution of flyers was more risky than participating in the demonstration in front of the Chinese consulate. The claimant responded that if he mentioned the flyer distribution he "would be implicated" as a member of Falun Gong. The panel rejects the claimant's explanation. The claimant filed a PIF in which he alleged that he has been a Falun Gong practitioner since 1994 and that he practiced Falun Gong in the same group as the member that was arrested. He also alleged in his PIF that he fled China because he was afraid of being arrested. It is reasonable to expect that the claimant would know that the disclosures he made in his PIF already "implicated" him as a member of Falun Gong. The panel finds the claimant's testimony in this regard neither plausible nor credible.

The claimant filed an amended PIF on October 5, 2011. The claimant was asked why he did not mention the distribution of flyers in his amended PIF. The claimant responded that he "didn't think it was important." The claimant testimony is inconsistent with his earlier testimony and in this regard, the panel draws a negative inference.

The claimant testified that there were 8 members in his Falun Gong group in China. The panel asked him how many members were arrested. The claimant responded that four members were arrested. The claimant went on to testify that one of the members was "persecuted to death", two others were seniors and they received one day in jail and a fine of 2000 yuan and that the fourth was sentenced to one month incarceration. The claimant was asked to name the individuals. The claimant provided four names, however, the claimant failed to state the name of the arrested person identified in his PIF. When the panel pointed out to the claimant that he failed to mention the person identified in his PIF, the claimant responded that the four members arrested were members of a different Falun Gong group of which he was a member. The panel rejects the claimant's explanation. The panel finds the claimant's testimony evolved in an effort to explain away an obvious inconsistency. In this regard the panel draws a negative inference.

It was noted by the panel that he omitted to mention in his PIF that he belonged to a second Falun Gong group in China and that four members were arrested resulting in the death of one of the members. The claimant's explanation was that he did not know the specific details of the persecution so he did not want to mention it because he would have difficultly explaining it at the hearing. The panel rejects the claimant's explanation. The claimant provided far more details of the four persons allegedly arrested than he did of the person mentioned in his PIF. The panel finds the claimant's explanation in this regard is not credible.

In addition, it was pointed out to the claimant that the PIF question number 31 specifically states that a claimant is to provide, among other things, details of "all the significant events" and measures taken against "similar situated persons." It is reasonable to expect if four members of the claimant's Falun Gong group were arrested and that one of the members was "persecuted to death" that the claimant would have mentioned it in his PIF regardless of how many details he had of the circumstances. The panel finds that the claimant's testimony that four members of his Falun Gong group were arrested and that one member was "persecuted to death" is not credible. The panel further finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant manufactured this testimony in a failed attempt to support his claim.

The claimant alleges in his PIF that the reason he fled China for Canada was that he feared that he would be arrested for his Falun Gong participation in China. However, the claimant testified that the PSB did not attend his home in China until XXX 2009, after he became involved in Falun Gong demonstrations in Canada. He testified that the PSB knew that he was in Canada when they attended his home. He further testified that the PSB warned his wife that if the claimant did not stop attending Falun Gong activities in Canada she would be arrested and that their son would be excluded from attending school. The panel notes that the claimant did not indicate in his PIF or his PIF amendment that the PSB had threatened to arrest his wife. The panel again notes that question 31 of the PIF specifically states that a claimant is to provide details on all measures taken against the claimant and the claimant's family. The panel draws a negative inference from the claimant's failure to mention that the PSB threatened to arrest his wife if he did not stop practicing Falun Gong in Canada.

The claimant's testimony is that despite the threats of the PSB, he continued to participate in very public demonstrations in Canada, including a demonstration in Ottawa during the visit of the Chinese president. Despite this, the claimant testimony is that no action has been taken against his wife and that his son continues to attend school without difficulty. The claimant testified that his family in China has not suffered any consequences as a result of his alleged participation in Falun Gong. Country documentary evidence4 indicates Falun Gong is considered a cult by the Chinese government and is banned. In addition, the documents indicate that Chinese authorities use the family of absconding practitioners as hostages to force the practitioner to give up the practice. If a practitioner and those who are accused of assisting practitioners do not cooperate with the authorities, the family is subject to punishment as well, including harassment, arbitrary interrogation, loss of job and loss of housing benefits. In the context of this case, where the absconding person has continued to participate in demonstrations in Canada contrary to the instructions of the PSB, it is reasonable to assume that the claimant's family would have experienced all or some of the punishments noted above. The panel notes that the claimant testified that the PSB have only attended his home in China and talked with his wife. The panel draws a negative inference from the claimant's family's continuing ability to carry on with their normal lives without facing consequences or interrogation at the hands of the PSB. In addition, the panel finds that the lack of action taken against the family of the claimant undermines the credibility of his testimony that the PSB is aware of his activities in Canada.

The claimant alleges that the PSB learned that he was in Canada because photographs of him protesting against the Chinese government were posted on Falun Gong associated websites. The claimant testified that no names associated to the photographs were included on the websites. The panel finds it unlikely that with over one billion citizens in China, Chinese authorities would be able to identify the claimant from a photograph on a website. The claimant has provided no evidence that he was known to the PSB for any reason. In fact, his testimony is that Chinese authorities believed that he had given up the practice of Falun Gong in 1999. In addition, according to his testimony, the PSB was not aware of his Falun Gong participation in China. In this regard, the panel draws a negative inference.

The claimant testified that the PSB did not ever allege that he participated in Falun Gong activities in China. He also testified that the PSB did not ever leave a summons or a warrant for him, nor did he allege that a summons was left for his parents. However, the claimant alleged in his PIF amendment that the PSB continue to search for him and his parents at their home in China. The claimant's testimony is inconsistent in this regard. The claimant testified that the PSB know that he is in Canada. He has also testified that the PSB has never alleged that he participated in Falun Gong activities in China and has only told his wife that he must stop his Falun Gong activities in Canada. Given the claimant's testimony that the only reason the PSB is interested in him is because of his Falun Gong activities in Canada, it is reasonable to believe that the PSB is not aware of his activities in China. The claimant alleges that he and his parents were similarly situated in China and as such, it is reasonable to believe that the PSB would also not be aware of his parents' Falun Gong activities. The panel draws a negative inference from the claimant's contradiction between the claimant's testimony and his amended PIF.

The panel also notes that the claimant has not produced any persuasive evidence that he is being pursed by the PSB. The sole basis for the claimant's allegation that he is being pursued by the PSB is his testimony and the allegations he had made in his Personal Information Form.

Based on the foregoing cumulative negative credibility findings and negative inferences drawn above, the lack of persuasive evidence and the claimant's own testimony, the panel finds the claimant's testimony that members of his Falun Gong groups in China were arrested, is not credible and that he is not being pursued by Chinese authorities for his alleged Falun Gong activities in China. Knowledge of Falun Gong

The claimant alleges he has been an active Falun Gong practitioner since 1994. In addition to practicing at home and in a group, the claimant alleges that he also read the book Zhuan Falun. Since being in Canada, the claimant alleges that he continues to practice in a group and testified that he continues to read Zhuan Falun daily. He alleges that when in China he read one "Talk" of Zhuan Falun per week since 1994. The panel notes that there are nine "Talks" in Zhuan Falun and given the claimant's testimony and, presuming he read each "Talk" the same number of times, he would have read each "Talk" approximately 45 times. As such, it is reasonable to expect that he would have a good understanding of the contents of Zhuan Falun and would be able to describe it with great detail.

The claimant was asked a number of questions regarding Falun Gong and Zhuan Falun. He was able to answer most questions; however, the panel finds that his responses did not reflect a level of knowledge that is consistent with a practitioner with over 17 years of continuous practice and extensive study of Zhuan Falun. In particular, the claimant identified "Talk" number 3 as his favourite "Talk"; however, he was not able to provide significant detail on the contents of the "Talk". He was able to identify some of the subtopics but did not provide any substance. In addition, the claimant was asked to identity five of the eight major distinguishing characteristics as described by Master Li in Zhuan Falun. The claimant was unable to provide one. His explanation was that he could not recall at the moment. It is reasonable to expect that given his alleged Falun Gong profile, he would know the major distinguishing characteristics. The panel finds it neither plausible nor credible that the claimant, who alleges that he has read Zhuan Falun to such an extent, would not know the major characteristics of Falun Gong.

While it is difficult to make a judgment regarding the genuineness of a claimant's beliefs it is necessary in this case. In doing so, the panel considered the totality of the evidence available. Although it is true the claimant does possess some knowledge of Falun Gong, it does not necessarily mean he is a genuine practitioner. Merely having some information regarding basic teachings and practice or the lack of such information does not necessarily reflect genuine or false practice. It is necessary to consider the totality of evidence available to the panel. The claimant provided a number of letters of support and a petition from individuals who claim that he is a genuine Falun Gong practitioner. The claimant also tendered photographs of his Falun Gong activities in Canada, including his participation at demonstrations. In addition, the claimant tendered a photocopy of a letter of support from XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX of the Falun Dafa Association.

The panel notes that none of the documents tendered provide evidence that the claimant became involved in the practice of Falun Gong immediately after arriving in Canada as he has alleged. The one exception is the photocopy of the letter from XXXXXXX. The letter states that "as soon as he arrived in Canada" the claimant "immediately exhibited a very strong understanding of Falun Gong". However the letter does not provide any information as to when the claimant arrived in Canada or how it became known to XXXXXXX. Furthermore, the letter does not state that XXXXXXX personally observed the claimant in the practice of Falun Gong or that he conducted a personal assessment of his genuineness. Counsel for the claimant argued that the Falun Dafa association only issued 7 letters in the previous year in support of practitioners and as such, the panel ought to give the tendering of such a letter considerable weight in the hearing. The panel is not persuaded by counsel's argument. The letter provided to the panel is a photocopy. It is reasonable to expect that given the Falun Dafa Association only issued seven letters in the past year that an original could have been obtained. In addition, the panel notes that counsel advised the panel at the start of the hearing that XXXXXXX was present at the Board and that although notice was not provided to the Board in advance, counsel was seeking to call him as a witness. After the panel conducted its questioning of the claimant, the panel provided counsel the opportunity to call Mr. XXXXX as a witness, however, counsel declined. In any event, these documents can only attest to the claimant's participation in Falun Gong activities; they do not attest to his motivation. In this regard, recent case law5 indicates that a pastor's assessment of the genuineness of a person's faith cannot be substituted for the assessment that the panel is required to make. In the same regard, the panel finds that the assessment of a Falun Gong practitioner cannot be substituted for the assessment the panel is required to make. For the foregoing reasons, the panel gives little evidentiary weight to these documents.

Having previously found that the claimant's Falun Gong group members were not arrested and that the claimant is not being pursued by the PSB for his Falun Gong activities in China, and in the context of his knowledge of Falun Gong, the panel finds that the claimant was not a genuine practitioner in China as he alleges. The panel further finds, on a balance of probabilities, and on the basis of the findings and negative inferences noted above, and in the context of his knowledge of Falun Gong, that the claimant's allegation that he was a genuine Falun Gong practitioner in China is not credible and was only for the purpose of supporting a fraudulent claim.

Having found that the claimant was not a Falun Gong practitioner in China, the panel must consider whether the claimant is a genuine Falun Gong practitioner in this county. The panel finds that it is reasonable to expect 'good faith' in making a refugee claim. In this regard, R.P.G. Haines, the Chairman of a refugee status appeal panel and A.G. Wang Heed, a member of the United Nations High Commission for Refugees stated in part: If there is no good faith requirement in the sur place situation, it places in the hands of the appellant for refugee status the means of unilaterally determining the grant to him or her of refugee status.6

In this regard, the panel cites the following from James Hathaway's The Law of Refugee Status with regard to "sur place" claims: "An individual who as a stratagem deliberately manipulates circumstances to create a real chance of persecution which did not exist cannot be said to belong to this category".7 The panel finds on a balance of probabilities that this claim has not been made in good faith.

Having found that the claimant was not a genuine Falun Gong practitioner in China and having found that this claim has not been made in good faith, the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, and in the context of findings noted above, that the claimant's participation in Falun Gong activities in Canada was only for the purpose of supporting a fraudulent refugee claim. The panel finds on a balance of probabilities that the claimant engaged in Falun Gong activities in Canada only to create the circumstances in which he could file a refugee protection claim.

In the context as noted above, as well as in the context of the cumulative findings and negative inferences noted above, the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant is not a genuine Falun Gong practitioner nor would he be perceived to be in China.

On the basis of the totality of the evidence and the cumulative findings, the panel finds that the claimant has not satisfied his burden of establishing a serious possibility that he would be persecuted or that he would be personally subjected to a risk to his life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture by any authority in the People's Republic of China.

The claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The Refugee Protection Division rejects his claim. (signed) "L. Favreau " L.
